justification: Three independent primary clinical reports provide variant-level human evidence: PMID 31794024 identified the homozygous TRAPPC4 c.454+3A>G splice variant in seven affected children from three unrelated families with early-onset seizures, microcephaly and spastic quadriparesis, with functional validation of splicing and trafficking/autophagy defects; PMID 32901138 independently replicated this in 23 patients from 17 unrelated families with early-onset epilepsy and progressive encephalopathy; and PMID 34878169 reported novel bi-allelic missense variants (c.191T>C, c.278C>T) in three individuals from two additional Indian families with seizures, extending the allelic spectrum beyond the recurrent variant. PMIDs 32125366/32125358 further corroborate the recurrent variant with muscle involvement. Supporting mechanistic work in yeast and fibroblasts (PMID 32116085) adds biological plausibility but is not needed for the human causal claim. Unrelated mentions (Parkinson eQTL, smallpox eQTL, FXS iPSC transcriptome) are incidental co-mentions.

justification: Multiple independent human studies report their own primary genetic findings: Oliver et al. (PMID 25401298) identified a recurrent de novo KCNC1 c.959G>A (p.Arg320His) in 11 unrelated exome-sequenced PME probands plus 2 in a replication cohort; Muona/Oliver follow-up of 20 MEAK patients (PMID 28380698) characterized the syndrome clinically and functionally; Cameron et al. (PMID 31353855) reported 10 new cases including six unrelated patients with de novo p.Ala421Val causing developmental and epileptic encephalopathy; Park et al. (PMID 31353862) found three further novel de novo variants in five unrelated individuals with myoclonic/generalized epilepsy. Additional independent probands and families (PMIDs 29428275 familial mosaicism, 34733949 p.R317S, 34232791 A513V in EIFMS, 34786481 three PME cases) replicate the association across distinct cohorts, supported by concordant loss-of-function electrophysiology. This constitutes strong, replicated human genetic evidence of causality across multiple epilepsy phenotypes.

justification: No article in this set reports LRRTM2 sequence variants in autism probands or families; ASD is mentioned only as background in papers whose own results concern neurexin–LRRTM2 binding, synapse organization, or other genes (e.g., NRXN1/NRXN2 truncating mutations in PMID 21424692, where LRRTM2 is merely the binding assay partner). The one human genetic study centered on LRRTM2 (PMID 23326251) concerns a multigene 5q31.2 microdeletion with ID/DD and explicitly found no relevant LRRTM2 point mutations in 330 ID/DD patients — a negative result that cannot support Existing, and a CNV spanning CTNNA1/LRRTM2 cannot implicate the gene alone. The LRRTM-family sequencing study (PMID 31854516) found associations only with LRRTM4 and for suicide attempt in bipolar disorder, not LRRTM2/ASD. Strong biological plausibility remains: LRRTM2 is a postsynaptic organizer binding neurexins and heparan sulfate, regulating excitatory synapse development, with mouse knockouts showing AMPAR/LTP deficits (PMIDs 20519524, 29784826, 30100184, 30262834), supporting Hypothesized.

justification: Every article provided concerns CHRNA1 in the context of the muscle nicotinic acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction: congenital myasthenic syndromes, autoimmune myasthenia gravis, fetal akinesia deformation sequence/multiple pterygium syndrome, and pregnancy loss. None of the abstracts mentions epilepsy, seizures, or any CNS/epileptic phenotype, and no variant in CHRNA1 is reported in patients with epilepsy. The gene's splicing biology (exon P3A, hnRNP L/PTB) and its disease associations are entirely peripheral/neuromuscular, giving no clear mechanistic basis for cortical hyperexcitability (unlike neuronal nicotinic subunits). A small residual probability is allotted to "Hypothesized" only because nicotinic acetylcholine receptor subunit biology is broadly relevant to excitability, but no supporting data appear here.

justification: Direct human genetic evidence is present and replicated: Geisheker/Salpietro-type cohort study (PMID 31300657) reported heterozygous de novo GRIA2 variants in 28 unrelated patients with intellectual disability and neurodevelopmental abnormalities explicitly including autism spectrum disorder, with supporting functional electrophysiology. Independent case reports provide replication in separate probands: a de novo missense variant (p.Lys530Met) in a boy with ASD, global developmental delay and epileptic encephalopathy (PMID 35534222), and a de novo p.Ala770Thr variant in a patient with atypical ASD and psychiatric symptoms (PMID 36329391); an iPSC line was derived from an ASD patient carrying a GRIA2 frameshift (PMID 35134694). Additional de novo loss-of-function and gain-of-function reports (PMID 32948840, 36161652, 34899870) describe the same NEDLIB spectrum with autistic features, consistent with a dominant single-gene mechanism rather than contiguous-gene effects (unlike the GLRB/GRIA2 deletion case, PMID 22669415, which cannot isolate the gene). Residual probability for "Existing" reflects that ASD is typically one feature within a broader developmental/epileptic phenotype rather than isolated ASD.

justification: Every article in this set concerns MYH2 as a skeletal muscle myosin heavy chain gene causing congenital/hereditary myopathies with ophthalmoplegia, dysphagia, and muscle weakness (e.g., PMIDs 11114175, 20418530, 23388406, 36380287); none reports autism spectrum disorder or any neurodevelopmental/behavioral phenotype attributable to MYH2 variants. The only tangential mention is a case report of a child with motor developmental delay and intellectual disability carrying MYH2 missense variants (PMID 30662633), but intellectual disability in the context of a myopathy is not ASD and no autism diagnosis or systematic evaluation is reported. Other co-mentions (PMID 30009132, 34439639) list MYH2 variants of uncertain significance incidentally in exome panels for mitochondrial or muscular disease, with no ASD relevance. There is no expression, pathway, or animal-model evidence linking MYH2 biology to autism in this corpus, so the relationship is best described as Novel, with a small allowance for a weak "hypothesized" reading via the ID case report.
